appDescription: Operations console for the Texas power grid: telemetry, forecasts, alarms and network topology.

notFound.title: Page not found
notFound.body: The page you are looking for does not exist.

offline.title: You are offline
offline.body: This page has not been saved on this device yet. Pages you have opened before, and your incident reports, work without a connection.

pwa.iosHint: To install, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen.
pwa.offline: You are offline. Pages and data you have opened before still work; live data resumes when you reconnect.

home.what: The front page of the console. It shows the latest figures for the real Texas power grid and a summary of the practice grid that the other pages use.
home.looking: The top cards are real numbers published by the U.S. Energy Information Administration: how much electricity Texas is using, what was forecast, and where the power comes from. Below them is a count of the made-up substations, power lines and power plants shown elsewhere.
home.how: Read it like a dashboard. Open a section from the menu to see more detail, and use this help button on any page to learn what it does.
home.why: Grid operators start each shift with a quick overview like this one: is demand normal, is the forecast holding, and is anything unusual going on?

telemetry.what: A very large table of readings from every piece of equipment on the practice grid, recorded every 15 minutes over six days.
telemetry.looking: Each row is one reading: which equipment it is, where it is, how hard it is working and whether that is normal. There are more than a million rows.
telemetry.how: Click a column title to sort. Use the filters to narrow the list, or group rows to see totals by area or type. Click a row to select that equipment; the other pages highlight it too.
telemetry.why: Operators use tables like this to find equipment that is overloaded or behaving oddly, and to check what happened at a given time.

charts.what: Line charts of the last 30 days on the Texas grid: how much electricity was used, what was forecast, how it was produced and how much came from neighbouring grids.
charts.looking: Real hourly data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, plus one practice series with a reading every second, about 2.6 million points.
charts.how: Zoom into any chart and drag to move through time. The other charts follow, so you can compare them at the same moment.
charts.why: Comparing demand with the forecast and with how power was produced shows when the grid was under strain and how it coped.

alarms.what: A live list of warnings from the practice grid, such as a power line carrying too much electricity or a voltage that is too low.
alarms.looking: New alarms appear as they happen. The counters at the top show how many are active and how many nobody has handled yet.
alarms.how: Filter by severity or area, and pause the feed to read without the list moving. Acknowledge an alarm to tell everyone else watching that you are dealing with it; they see it straight away.
alarms.why: In a real control room, alarms are how operators learn that something needs attention. Acknowledging them stops two people chasing the same problem.

map.what: A map of Texas with every substation, power plant, customer area and power line of the practice grid.
map.looking: Colours show how heavily each piece of equipment is loaded right now, updated live. The legend explains the colours, and the layer switches hide or show each kind of equipment.
map.how: Zoom and drag the map like any online map. Click a dot or a line to select it and see its details; the other pages highlight it too. Choose Show as table for a list of everything on the map.
map.why: Seeing where the strain is helps operators understand a problem at a glance, for example several busy lines in the same region.

network.what: The practice grid drawn as a network: which substations are connected to which, and through which power lines.
network.looking: A tree lists every area and piece of equipment, and a diagram draws the connections. Line colours show either live loading or the result of a what-if study.
network.how: Select equipment in the tree or the diagram. In the what-if study, trip a line, take equipment offline or change a load, and see how the power would flow after the change. Undo or reset at any time.
network.why: Before taking a line out for repairs, engineers check that the rest of the grid can carry the extra power. This page shows that check in a simple form.

incidents.what: Written reports about events on the grid, for example an outage or a piece of equipment that failed.
incidents.looking: A list of reports with their status and severity. A sample report shows what a finished one looks like.
incidents.how: Create a report, link the equipment involved, add follow-up actions and attach PDF documents. Reports are saved in this browser only; nothing is sent anywhere.
incidents.why: Writing down what happened, and what will be done about it, is how teams learn from incidents and stop them happening again.
